title: Commit and publish to remote
first_prompt: Commit and publish all work to remote. Note: this is the first commit from this new VM environment, flag any potential setup issues for review

commits.summary: Installer runs Dafny and Boogie on hosts with only .NET 10
commits.body: On Ubuntu 26.04 only the .NET 10 runtime is packaged, and Boogie (built for .NET 8) refuses to start. When no .NET 8 runtime is present, install.sh now writes launchers for dafny and boogie into ~/.local/bin, ahead of ~/.dotnet/tools on PATH, that set DOTNET_ROLL_FORWARD=Major. gh_asset also now prints nothing (rather than the string "null") when no release asset matches, so a fallback written as $(a || b) receives only the other URL. Verified on a fresh Ubuntu 26.04.1 VM with only Microsoft.NETCore.App 10.0.14: bash -n passes, dafny --version reports 4.11.0 and boogie starts through the launcher, and the new jq filter returns the first matching URL or exits 4 with no output on a sample release JSON.
Brings the published traces up to this point: conversation that came after a session's last commit, and sessions with no commit of their own.

commits.summary: Verification report names the machine of every result and calibrates estimates per machine
commits.body: Results already recorded their host and environment, but the Markdown report showed neither and pooled every machine into one calibration table. Until now every result came from one 8-core aarch64 WSL2 laptop; the queue is now running on a 28-vCPU x86_64 VM, so durations from the two would mix. report now labels each result with its machine (host, architecture, WSL, CPUs), the JSON report gains a machine field per result and a calibrationByHost table (calibration keeps its old pooled shape), and the Markdown report prints one calibration table per machine. verification/README.md records which machine ran which results and no longer calls the WSL laptop 'this machine'. Verified with the pipeline's unit tests (22 pass, one extended to check the label and the per-host table) and by rendering the report over the 88 collected results.

commits.summary: Results record the runner's machine name, and the installer provides jsonschema
commits.body:
A new runner setting, machine_name (verification/pipeline.toml, empty by default; set per machine in pipeline.local.toml), is what a result records as runner.host and environment.host, and what the note in a truncated log names, in place of the hostname. This lets machines be aliased as more VMs or cloud runners are added, without publishing hostnames, which the trace redactor already treats as personal. Claims in the runner's local state keep the real hostname, which they need to recognise their own stale claims. The VM now running the queue is named vm-1 in its local config; results from the WSL laptop keep its hostname, FilSurface, as before.

The first run on the VM failed 26 of its first 50 jobs within a second, all because the Python module jsonschema was missing: build.py publishes no example result it cannot validate. The Ubuntu installer now installs python3-jsonschema and doctor.sh checks it. Verified: the pipeline's unit tests pass (23, with a new test that a configured machine name is recorded in both host fields and the truncated-log note, and the hostname nowhere in the result); doctor.sh reports jsonschema 4.19.2 on the VM.

commits.summary: Record verification results for 60 jobs, the first run on the vm-1 VM
commits.body:
Every job that was pending ran on vm-1, a 28-vCPU x86_64 VM (Ubuntu 26.04), under a budget of 12 workers, 24 CPUs and 32 GiB; all earlier results came from the 8-core aarch64 WSL laptop. 54 passed and 6 failed. A first attempt was set aside unrecorded: 26 of its jobs failed because Python's jsonschema module was missing on the VM (now installed by the setup script), and its results named the VM by hostname. TLC results for examples 072, 074, 083, 093 and 099 were reused from checkpoints that attempt left on the same machine, under identical inputs, as their results record, so those jobs' times are not measurements.

Findings for the submitters: both conformance corpus jobs (20261106-021741, 20261106-024336) fail with disagreements with the JVM. Under --gaps strict JBMC says Verified for capacity, builderCapacity, mapCapacity, setCapacity and loadFactor, which the JVM refutes, and under auto --confirm the own checker reports violations on caught(n=0) and nestedHandler(n=0) that the JVM does not reproduce (10 and 12 disagreements). Examples 147, 148 and 149 stop before any proof: their patches create the subject file Jitter.java, and build.py's excerpt of a patch requires the subject to exist before it, at the jobs' commits and still at this one. Job 20261105-235249 (example 142 killed mid-proof) failed on the machine, not on build.py: its step expects GNU timeout's exit status 137 after -s KILL, and the uutils coreutils Ubuntu 26.04 ships returns 124.

Outputs of 43 jobs were not applied, because their files changed after the jobs' commits; they are kept under each result's outputs/. Most short B8, B9 and B11 runs were throttled by a 1-CPU estimate. The applied outputs regenerated examples/README.md and examples/index.json.

commits.summary: The verification runner stops a step past its timeout only when it has stalled; the installer puts GNU coreutils first on Ubuntu 26.04
commits.body:
A job's timeout used to be a deadline: at 4 times its estimate (at least 5 minutes) a step was stopped, working or not. Estimates are often far off, and a long run is information about the change and the machine, so the timeout is now where the runner starts looking for a hang. Past it, a step is stopped only once it has stalled: under 1% of a CPU (read from its cgroup, or from /proc for its session without one) and no new log output for stall_window, 10 minutes by default. A step still working is left to finish, and the result marks it overranTimeout with an attention line. Only max_timeout (6h by default) stops a step that is still working; stoppedFor says which rule stopped one. Results record both settings.

Ubuntu 26.04 ships the Rust uutils as its coreutils, and jobs noticed: timeout exits 124 rather than GNU's 137 after -s KILL, which failed the job for example 142 killed mid-proof. build-essential depends on coreutils-from-uutils there, so the installer does not switch system-wide; it links GNU's gnu-prefixed binaries under their own names into ~/.local/lib/gnu-coreutils and puts that first on PATH in .bashrc, .profile (a non-interactive login shell stops early in .bashrc) and .zshrc. doctor.sh fails when timeout is not GNU's, and every result now records the coreutils its job saw.

commits.summary: Rerun 39 verification jobs at this commit on vm-1 (verification pending)
commits.body: The first run on the VM left the outputs of 43 jobs unapplied, because the example files they wrote had changed since the jobs' commits. Each distinct one is resubmitted to run at this commit (38 jobs; four exact duplicates and the superseded benchmark are left out), with 2 CPUs for those that asked for 1, since their JVM runs spent 30-93% of their time held back by the quota. The job for example 142 killed mid-proof is resubmitted unchanged: it failed only on uutils timeout's exit status, and GNU coreutils now come first on the VM's PATH. Examples 147-149 and the two conformance corpora are not rerun: their failures are deterministic findings for their authors.

commits.summary: Setup for Ubuntu moves to examples/setup/ubuntu, with every difference between 24.04 and 26.04 decided in one place
commits.body: The installer was named for WSL, but only two preflight warnings concern WSL; it serves Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 on machines, VMs and WSL2 alike, so examples/setup/ubuntu-wsl is now examples/setup/ubuntu. What differs between the releases used to be found out step by step, by probing apt or the installed tools. It is now set by one case on VERSION_ID, release_profile: the .NET SDK package (8 or 10), whether Dafny and Boogie get roll-forward launchers (26.04 only), the QEMU packages, the releases whose CBMC .deb to try in order (26.04 falls back to 24.04's), and whether GNU coreutils go first on PATH (26.04 only). Each step reads only those settings, and a release with no case stops the installer instead of warning and carrying on. The setup README lists the differences in a table.

commits.summary: Record the open JBMC soundness findings and the stuck Crosscut examples where the next session will look
commits.body:
The two conformance corpus jobs (1d, 1e) came back failing, and Phase 1 of llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md, which read as complete apart from them, is not done. Under --gaps strict JBMC says Verified for seven claims the JVM refutes: four JDK constructors given a negative capacity and HashMap's load factor (its 2022 library models return normally), synchronized (null), Random.nextBytes and a record's equals through invokedynamic. --engine auto passes two of them through where the own checker has no verdict. JBMC also reports violations the JVM does not reproduce on caught(n=0) and nestedHandler(n=0), which catch the ArithmeticException of a division by zero. The brief's Progress now records each disagreement with its job id, what closing Phase 1 needs, and that the two jobs, rerun unchanged, are the acceptance test.

Examples 147, 148 and 149 never reached a proof: their patches create the subject file, which build.py's excerpts() does not accept. Each example's notes, and the brief, say so and what would unblock them. Nothing was fixed; this records the work so that it is not lost before it is taken up.

commits.summary: Record verification results for the 39 jobs rerun on vm-1: all pass
commits.body: The jobs resubmitted at e9763b54, to refresh outputs a run at older commits could not apply, all passed on vm-1, with GNU coreutils on PATH (each result now records it). The job for example 142 killed mid-proof, which had failed only because the uutils timeout exits 124 rather than 137 after -s KILL, passes: build.py leaves its claim, patched copy and stage log behind when killed mid-stage. Ten jobs left two outputs each unapplied, because several jobs of the run wrote the same example's README.md and result.json and the first one applied changed them for the rest; each of those 14 files was applied from another job of this run at the same commit, so every example is current. The applied outputs regenerated examples/README.md and examples/index.json.
Brings the published traces up to this point: conversation that came after a session's last commit, and sessions with no commit of their own.

commits.summary: Verification findings that need a person go into verification/findings.md, kept by the agent that runs the pipeline
commits.body:
A run's findings lived in its results, its commit message and the managing session's report, and the last two are easy to lose before anyone acts. verification/findings.md is now the durable list: each entry (VF-NNN) records a verdict against a change, an error a submitter must fix, or a decision that changes what the results mean, with its jobs, commit and machine, what was found, what would settle it and who should act, where else it is tracked, and the check that closes it. Open entries come first.

It starts with the two open findings from the first runs on vm-1: VF-001, the conformance corpus jobs where JBMC proves claims the JVM refutes, reports violations the JVM does not reproduce, and --engine auto passes JBMC's wrong Verified through (Phase 1 of the sound-verdicts brief is not done); and VF-002, examples 147-149, whose patches create their subject file, which build.py's excerpts() does not accept. The run-verification skill gains a Record step (add, update, close; never close on a job that did not run the named check), reads open entries before a run, commits the file with the results and names entries in its report. The unattended verification loop's instruction and the verification README say the same.
Brings the published traces up to this point: conversation that came after a session's last commit, and sessions with no commit of their own.
